title: Extreme heat is becoming a household cost and daily-routine problem while public cooling access and health knowledge lag
source_unit: Annenberg Science and Public Health Survey wave 30; SSRS nationally representative panel of 1,904 U.S. adults, August 4–17, 2026
geography: United States; nationally representative adults ages 18 and older

observations.period: August 2026; climate, heat, and household exposure

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the 30th wave of the Annenberg Science and Public Health Survey

extreme_heat_affected_daily_activities.unit: percent reporting at least sometimes in the past year

wildfire_smoke_air_quality_affected_dail.unit: percent reporting at least sometimes in the past year

climate_change_increases_health_risk.unit: percent saying climate change increases heat-, respiratory-, and insect-borne illness risk

observations.method: Nationally representative ASAPH/SSRS web-and-telephone survey weighted to the U.S. adult population; full-sample margin of error ±3.2 percentage points.
observations.uncertainty: These are self-reported experiences and beliefs; they do not establish local meteorological exposure, health diagnoses, or causal effects of climate change on an individual respondent.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reported heat and smoke impacts vary with location, recall, health, housing, work, mobility, and media awareness; broad climate-risk recognition does not imply uniform policy preferences or preparedness.

observations.period: August 2025–August 2026; household expenses and extreme-heat routines

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the 30th wave of the Annenberg Science and Public Health Survey

unexpected_weather_related_utility_expen.unit: percent reporting unexpected utility expenses caused by storms, flooding, heat, or wildfires

heat_impacted_electricity_bills.unit: percent reporting major or minor impact

heat_impacted_outdoor_activities.unit: percent reporting major or minor impact

heat_impacted_exercise.unit: percent reporting major or minor impact

heat_impacted_sleep.unit: percent reporting major or minor impact

observations.method: ASAPH/SSRS survey estimates of self-reported household expense and lifestyle impacts, with comparison to August 2025.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not isolate heat from other weather events for utility expenses, establish dollar amounts, or identify whether changes in sleep and exercise reflect heat, smoke, work schedules, health, or other conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Adaptation can shift rather than eliminate costs—for example, from outdoor activity to electricity or air conditioning—and reported lifestyle impact is not equivalent to clinical harm.

observations.period: August 2025–August 2026; air quality response and cooling access

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the 30th wave of the Annenberg Science and Public Health Survey

local_unhealthy_air_quality.unit: percent saying local authorities reported unhealthy air days in the prior three months

stayed_indoors_after_air_warning.unit: percent among those reporting unhealthy air who stayed indoors more than usual

used_air_conditioning.unit: percent among those reporting unhealthy air

used_air_purifier.unit: percent among those reporting unhealthy air

observations.method: ASAPH/SSRS survey estimates of local air-quality experience, reported responses, and cooling-center knowledge.
observations.uncertainty: Air-quality exposure is based on respondent awareness of local health-authority reports; the survey does not measure cooling-center availability, distance, accessibility, capacity, or actual use.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults ages 18 and older; response measures are conditioned on those reporting unhealthy air days where specified.
observations.counterinterpretation: Indoor sheltering, air conditioning, purifiers, masks, and cooling centers are unequal adaptation options; low cooling-center awareness may reflect communication gaps, lack of nearby facilities, or non-applicability.

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the 30th wave of the Annenberg Science and Public Health Survey

recognize_dizziness.unit: percent identifying dizziness as a heat-illness sign

know_heat_pregnancy_preterm_risk.unit: percent correctly identifying greater early-delivery risk for pregnant people exposed to extreme heat

observations.method: ASAPH/SSRS knowledge questions on heat-illness symptoms and pregnancy risk.
observations.uncertainty: Correct-response shares measure survey knowledge, not recognition or action during an actual heat event; medical guidance and individual risk vary by condition and context.
observations.counterinterpretation: People may know common symptoms while missing less intuitive signs or pregnancy-specific risks; knowledge alone does not establish access to care, cooling, or ability to change conditions.

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the 30th wave of the Annenberg Science and Public Health Survey

expect_greater_heat_stroke_risk.unit: percent expecting greater community heat-stroke risk in next 10 years

identify_older_adults_as_most_vulnerable.unit: percent identifying adults 65 and older as the group with most heat-related deaths

observations.method: ASAPH/SSRS survey estimates of perceived future risk and knowledge of vulnerable populations.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived future risk is not a forecast and vulnerability knowledge does not measure whether communities have targeted protections, resources, or trusted communication.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stable risk perception can coexist with changing lived exposure; recognizing older-adult vulnerability does not imply awareness of risks for pregnant people, outdoor workers, children, or people without cooling.

related_sources.claim: NOAA context for the record summer referenced by APPC.

boundary: This record captures U.S. public experience, knowledge, and perceptions of extreme heat, wildfire smoke, climate-health risk, household costs, routines, cooling access, and vulnerability. It does not establish clinical outcomes, local exposure, adaptation effectiveness, distributional causality, or whether public awareness produces protective action.
